extracted.intended_audience: administrative-law scholars, judges, and practitioners (including law students and agency counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and doctrinal criteria for when courts should invalidate agency action versus hold agency errors harmless (harmless-error analysis, remand-without-vacatur, injunction scope, severability, notice-and-comment defects, Chenery/adequate-reasoning issues). Written as a law-review treatment aimed at rethinking remedial doctrine across administrative law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of prejudicial error / harmless-error review
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA instructs that “due account shall be taken of the rule of prejudicial error,” i.e., errors that have no substantial bearing on the ultimate rights of the parties will be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmless-error review should allow courts to hold agency mistakes harmless where they did not affect the decision; courts should ask whether the agency’s mistake materially frustrated the values the procedure was meant to serve. The Article notes the rule’s textual grounding (5 U.S.C. § 706) and historical pedigree (Attorney General’s Manual), but observes the rule has been largely forgotten by modern administrative law and the Supreme Court only recently engaged the provision (e.g., Nat’l Ass’n of Home Builders v. Defs. of Wildlife; Shinseki v. Sanders). Examples and anti-patterns: courts rarely apply harmlessness in practice; the prevailing approach is to presume prejudice and vacate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default remedy of vacatur and remand
rubrics_metrics.description: When a court determines that an agency action violates the APA, the conventional remedy is to invalidate (vacate) the action and remand to the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule-bound default aims to encourage procedural fastidiousness and protect against agency evasion of legal constraints, but it can be disproportionately harsh. The Article critiques reflexive vacatur as often excessive, costly, and disruptive of beneficial programs, and warns it can produce perverse doctrinal effects (e.g., courts may narrow substantive review to avoid invalidation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand without vacatur (retain rule in force while remanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remanding an agency action without vacating it when defects are modest and invalidation would be disruptive (a practice developed by the D.C. Circuit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by cases like Allied-Signal, Inc. v. U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Comm’n; justified by reference to the APA’s prejudicial-error instruction. Controversial and opposed by judges who view it as unlawfully substituting the court’s decision for the agency’s (see Milk Train, Inc. v. Veneman; Checkosky v. SEC). The Article argues remand-without-vacatur can be lawful and useful when vacatur would impose disproportionate costs and the errors are insubstantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-comment harmlessness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Circuits typically hold that failure to provide notice and comment is harmless only where the agency’s mistake 'clearly had no bearing on the procedure used or the substance of decision reached.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Riverbend Farms v. Madigan and applied in many circuits (Allina, Animal Legal Def. Fund, U.S. Steel). The Article urges courts to look beyond formal compliance and ask whether the informational and participatory functions of § 553 were materially frustrated. Factors: whether the challenger knew what the agency intended, whether the agency solicited or received equivalent input through other channels, whether the agency addressed those concerns, and whether missing comments would likely have changed the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational and participatory functions of notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment serves informational functions (ensure agency incorporates relevant information) and participatory functions (give the public a voice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmlessness inquiry should test whether those functions were frustrated: Did the agency inform affected parties of its intent? Did it open lines of communication? What comments would have been submitted and would they have mattered? The Article documents extensive informal agency solicitation (listening sessions, workshops, leaks) and urges courts to consider such alternative channels when assessing prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical outgrowth / legislative vs. nonlegislative rule classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an agency action is a legislative rule (requiring notice-and-comment) or a nonlegislative action affects remedial analysis; questions about logical outgrowth can produce reasonable disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an agency reasonably believes a rule is exempt or that a final rule is a logical outgrowth of the proposal, a court that disagrees should consider whether invalidation actually improves future agency behavior. The Article suggests that where classification disputes are reasonable and the absence of formal proceedings did not frustrate notice-and-comment values, holding the error harmless may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause exemption evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may invoke 'good cause' to bypass pre-promulgation notice-and-comment; courts scrutinize such claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When courts find no good cause but the agency reasonably believed it existed (or the error was insubstantial), the remedial inquiry should ask whether vacatur is necessary. The Article cautions that a strong presumption against post-promulgation cure exists (Hickman & Thomson), but urges assessment of whether the agency’s conduct materially harmed notice-and-comment values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chenery/adequate explanation requirement and harmlessness
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Chenery, agencies must supply a reasoned explanation for decisions at the time of decision; failure may render action invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower courts often invalidate actions infected by Prill-type or Chenery-type failures to give adequate reasons. But harmless-error analysis should apply where the record shows the agency’s error did not affect the outcome or the agency would not change its view on remand. The Article recommends regularizing when Chenery defects can be treated as harmless rather than automatically fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failures to resolve statutory ambiguities / interpretive errors
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency's statutory interpretation is erroneous, courts must decide whether that error requires invalidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the mistake stems from reasonable disagreement about the application of open-ended standards, invalidation may not improve future agency application; courts should consider harmlessness when the agency would likely reaffirm its interpretation on remand and when vacatur would be wasteful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptively prejudicial categories (agency acts beyond legal authority or avoids scrutiny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some errors should presumptively be treated as prejudicial: e.g., when an agency has acted beyond its legal authority or when an agency skipped notice-and-comment to avoid public scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article emphasizes that such errors are different in kind and generally warrant vacatur because there is no point asking if the agency would have reached the same decision if it had acted within authority or with public scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability and partial invalidation
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies adopt a rule that exceeds authority or contains illegal provisions, courts must decide whether to invalidate the entire rule or sever offending provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should consider severance as a remedial tool when offending provisions are severable and vacatur would be unduly disruptive. The Article points to literature on severability clauses and suggests more flexible remedial approaches here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and tailoring of injunctive relief (nationwide vs. limited injunctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunctions should be narrowly tailored; courts should consider limiting relief to particular plaintiffs rather than imposing nationwide injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article questions the practice of broad nationwide injunctions (citing Nat’l Mining Ass’n and scholarship by Samuel Bray) and suggests courts often should confine injunctive relief to those actually injured or otherwise narrowly fashion the remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stays to allow political branches to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: When courts rule against the government, they may enter stays to permit the political branches to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited example: the Supreme Court’s stay in N. Pipeline Constr. Co. v. Marathon Pipe Line Co. The Article proposes stays as a remedial device to reduce disruption and enable legislative or executive fixing of defects before vacatur takes effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual inquiry about whether an agency would have acted differently
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedial judgments require counterfactual assessments: would the agency have made a different choice had it adhered to procedure or provided better reasons?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although difficult, courts routinely engage in such counterfactuals in other contexts (e.g., harmless error in trials, exclusionary-rule balancing). The Article urges courts to confront these questions rather than avoid them via bright-line vacatur rules; bifurcation and remand-stage inquiries can help develop the factual record for remedial assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternative channels of public input and agency practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies frequently solicit input outside formal notice-and-comment (listening sessions, workshops, meetings, informal discussions, leaks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should factor such informal solicitation and post-promulgation comment/responses into the harmlessness analysis—did the agency effectively obtain the information and participation that notice-and-comment aims to produce?

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic incentives and magnitude-of-effect inquiry (sign fallacy/focusing illusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether changing remedial doctrine would meaningfully alter agency incentives and behavior; beware assuming small doctrinal tweaks have large systemic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article warns against the 'sign fallacy' (worrying about direction without assessing magnitude) and the 'focusing illusion'; courts should weigh whether modest remedial flexibility would realistically induce widespread procedural shirking before insisting on automatic vacatur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding doctrinal distortion to escape harsh remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may water down substantive review standards to avoid a remedy that seems disproportionate to perceived error (i.e., lowering the stringency of arbitrariness review to avoid vacatur).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an anti-pattern: remedial harshness can warp substantive doctrine. The Article argues for acknowledging remedial costs openly rather than disguising them through doctrinal change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bifurcated proceedings to separate merits and remedial inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts could order split proceedings—decide merits first, then conduct a separate remedial phase to determine appropriate relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bifurcation is common in civil litigation and would allow courts to develop a record on remedial questions (e.g., whether error was prejudicial) without conflating merits briefing with remedy issues. The Article cites Daugirdas recommending bifurcated hearings and gives Michigan v. EPA / White Stallion as an incidental example.
